primary_sources: Elizabeth Bentley, testimony before the House Committee on Un-American Activities, 1948

source: original; stimulus paraphrased from Elizabeth Bentley's testimony before HUAC, 1948

stimulus.source_note: Paraphrase of Elizabeth Bentley's testimony before the House Committee on Un-American Activities, 1948. Paraphrased, not quoted, because the source is after 1929.
stimulus.text: In 1948, Elizabeth Bentley, a former courier for a Soviet spy ring, testified before the House Committee on Un-American Activities. She named government employees she said had passed her secret information, including material on aircraft production, for delivery to Soviet agents. The committee used her testimony to open a wider investigation of communists in the government.

stem: The committee's use of Bentley's testimony best illustrates which feature of the Second Red Scare?

options.text: Congress waited for courts to convict spies before investigating anyone.
options.misconception: HUAC investigated first and let accusations lead. Background from the books: courts convicted Hiss of perjury only after the committee's hearings had made the case famous.

options.text: One witness's claims could open wide investigations of loyalty.
The committee ignored claims of espionage in the government.
options.misconception: Background from the books: the committee built its work on espionage claims, including Bentley's and Chambers's. Ignoring them would have left HUAC with no cases at all.

options.text: The public demanded that HUAC stop its investigations.
options.misconception: Background from the books: the public supported the hunt in the late 1940s, and HUAC's hearings drew wide attention. Demands to stop the committee came later, after McCarthy's fall.

rationales.A: HUAC investigated first and let accusations lead. Background from the books: Hiss was convicted of perjury only after the committee's hearings had made the case famous.
rationales.B: Bentley's claims about a spy ring led the committee to investigate communists across the government. A single witness's story opened a much wider hunt.
rationales.C: Background from the books: the committee built its work on espionage claims, including Bentley's and Chambers's. Ignoring them would have left HUAC with no cases at all.
rationales.D: Background: the public supported the hunt in the late 1940s, and HUAC's hearings drew wide attention. Demands to stop the committee came later, after McCarthy's fall.
rationales.general:
1. Bentley was one witness with a story about a spy ring and named government employees.
2. HUAC used her story to open a wider investigation of communists across the government.
3. That widening is the pattern of the era: one accusation licensed many more investigations, and each new name produced still more names to chase.
Remember: In a scare, one accusation can license many more.
